claim: The C. elegans hermaphrodite nervous system contains 302 neurons classified into 118 anatomically distinct classes.
source: The 302 neurons of the nervous system of the hermaphrodite have been classified into 118 anatomically distinct classes (Hobert et al., 2016; White et al., 1986).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hobert et al., 2016 and White et al., 1986

claim: Cholinergic motor neurons in the C. elegans ventral nerve cord can be divided into seven classes: DA, DB, SAB, AS, VA, VB, and VC.
source: As shown in Figure 1A, these cholinergic MNs can be divided into seven classes, the embryonically generated DA, DB, and SAB, and the post-embryonically generated AS, VA, VB and VC classes (Von Stetina et al., 2006; White et al., 1976).
evidence: Supported by citations to Von Stetina et al., 2006 and White et al., 1976, and shown in Figure 1A

claim: Each motor neuron class is defined by unique morphology shared by all class members that intermingle along the anterior-posterior axis.
source: Each MN class is defined by its unique morphology that is shared by each individual class member (DA = 9 class members, DB = 7, SAB = 3, VA = 12, VB = 11, VC = 6, AS = 11) that intermingle along the A-P axis (Figure 1A).
evidence: Stated in text and illustrated in Figure 1A

claim: Motor neuron classes are traditionally defined by class-specific axodendritic projection patterns and synaptic connectivity patterns.
source: Traditionally, each one of these MN classes has been defined by a combination of class-specific axodendritic projection patterns and class specific patterns of synaptic connectivity (White et al., 1986).
evidence: Supported by citation to White et al., 1986

claim: Motor neuron classes express unique combinations of effector genes that assign unique features to each class.
source: This classification is corroborated by the class-specific expression of a unique combination of effector genes that assign unique features to each MN class (Hobert et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hobert et al., 2016

claim: Motor neuron class-specific genes include genes encoding neurotransmitter receptors, ion channels, gap junction proteins and signaling molecules.
source: These include genes encoding neurotransmitter receptors, ion channels, gap junction proteins and signaling molecules (Figure 1B).
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 1B

claim: The C. elegans wiring diagram reveals correlation of connectivity differences with motor neuron cell body position along the anterior-posterior axis.
source: First, the C. elegans wiring diagram reveals a correlation of connectivity differences with MN cell body position along the A-P axis and, more specifically, with the location of individual class members in the retrovesicular ganglion, VNC and preanal ganglion.
evidence: Based on analysis of the C. elegans wiring diagram

claim: DA8 and DA9 neurons display several synaptic connectivity differences compared to DA1-DA7 neurons.
source: For example, although all nine members of the DA neuron class share multiple connectivity features, such as input from the command (pre-motor) interneurons AVA and AVD and output to dorsal body wall muscle, the DA neurons located in the preanal ganglion (DA8 and DA9) display several synaptic connectivity differences when compared to the more anteriorly located DA neurons (DA1-DA7) which are located in the VNC and retrovesicular ganglion (Figure 1B, Figure 1—source data 1; www.wormwiring.org).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—source data 1, and reference to www.wormwiring.org

claim: unc-4 and unc-37 are selectively required in VA neurons located in the VNC but not in the retrovesicular ganglion or preanal ganglion.
source: A paired-type homeobox gene, unc-4, and a Groucho corepressor, unc-37, are selectively required only in VA neurons located in the VNC (VA2-VA10), but not in the retrovesicular ganglion (VA1) or preanal ganglion (VA11,VA12) to specify the correct pattern of presynaptic input from AVA pre-motor neurons (Miller et al., 1992; Pflugrad et al., 1997; White et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to Miller et al., 1992; Pflugrad et al., 1997; White et al., 1992

claim: The TGFβ-like molecule unc-129 is selectively expressed in DA1-7 neurons but not in DA8 and DA9 neurons.
source: For example, as shown in Figure 1B, the TGFβ-like molecule unc-129 is selectively expressed in the DA neurons of the retrovesicular ganglion and VNC (DA1-7) and not in DA8 and DA9 neurons in the preanal ganglion (Colavita et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Colavita et al., 1998 and shown in Figure 1B

claim: The itr-1 gene is exclusively expressed in DA9.
source: Conversely, the itr-1 gene is exclusively expressed in DA9 (Klassen and Shen, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Klassen and Shen, 2007

claim: Posterior-most motor neuron class members generate unique electrical and/or chemical synaptic connections.
source: While MN class members located in the VNC or the preanal ganglion share many synaptic partners (schematically shown in Figure 1B and summarized in Figure 1—source data 1), several of the posterior-most MN class members generate unique electrical and/or chemical synaptic connections (Figure 1B, Figure 1—source data 1)(White et al., 1986).
evidence: Supported by citation to White et al., 1986 and data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—source data 1

claim: Posterior-most motor neuron class members receive selective input from tail sensory neurons.
source: In the tail, several of these subclass-specific synaptic connections are inputs from tail sensory neurons.
evidence: Based on analysis of synaptic connectivity patterns

claim: Selective sensory input enables posterior motor neurons to integrate information from the head with information from the tail.
source: This selective input presumably enables individual, posterior-most MN class members to integrate information received from the head (via command/pre-motor interneurons that innervate all MN class members) with information from the tail, thereby providing unique control of tail muscle.
evidence: Logical inference from connectivity patterns

claim: 68 male-specific neurons are generated exclusively in the male tail during sexual maturation in late larval stages.
source: During sexual maturation in late larval stages, 68 male-specific sensory, inter- and motor neurons are generated exclusively in the male tail (Sulston et al., 1980).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sulston et al., 1980

claim: The posterior-most members of all five cholinergic VNC motor neuron classes make extensive synaptic connections with male-specific neurons.
source: The posterior-most members of all five cholinergic VNC MN classes make extensive synaptic connections with these male-specific neurons (Jarrell et al., 2012) (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jarrell et al., 2012 and data in Figure 1—source data 1

claim: There are sexual dimorphisms in the synaptic connections that posterior-most VNC motor neuron subclasses make with sex-shared neurons.
source: Moreover, there are sexual dimorphisms in the synaptic connections that the posterior-most VNC MN subclasses make with neurons that are present in both sexes (Jarrell et al., 2012; White et al., 1986).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jarrell et al., 2012 and White et al., 1986

claim: The sex-shared AVG interneurons innervate DA9 only in males.
source: For example, the sex-shared AVG interneurons innervate DA9 only in males (Figure 1B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1B and supported by connectivity data

claim: The sex-shared PHB sensory neuron innervates VA12 only in hermaphrodites.
source: Vice-versa, the sex-shared PHB sensory neuron innervates VA12 only in hermaphrodites (Figure 1B) (Jarrell et al., 2012; White et al., 1986).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1B and supported by citations to Jarrell et al., 2012 and White et al., 1986

claim: The terminal selector transcription factor UNC-3 controls the identity of all distinct motor neuron classes.
source: We describe that the terminal selector-type transcription factor UNC-3, which controls the identity of all distinct MN classes (Kratsios et al., 2015, 2011), is also required for the expression of MN subclass-specific features.
evidence: Supported by citations to Kratsios et al., 2015, 2011

claim: UNC-3 is required for the expression of motor neuron subclass-specific features.
source: We describe that the terminal selector-type transcription factor UNC-3, which controls the identity of all distinct MN classes (Kratsios et al., 2015, 2011), is also required for the expression of MN subclass-specific features.
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis in this study

claim: UNC-3 activity is counteracted by class-specific repressor proteins to generate interclass diversity.
source: In regard to the specification of different MN classes, we have previously described that the activity of UNC-3 is counteracted by class-specific repressor proteins, resulting in 'interclass diversity' (Figure 1C)(Kerk et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kerk et al., 2017 and illustrated in Figure 1C

claim: UNC-3 requires region-specific cofactors in the form of Hox proteins to co-activate subclass-specific motor neuron features along the anterior-posterior axis.
source: In contrast, for 'subclass diversification', that is, diversification of subclasses within a given MN class (schematized in Figure 1C), we find that UNC-3 requires region-specific cofactors in the form of Hox proteins to co-activate subclass-specific MN features along the A-P axis.
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis in this study and illustrated in Figure 1C

claim: The neuronal IgCAM molecule rig-4 is expressed in all individual members of a given motor neuron class.
source: Confirming the notion that all neurons of a given class share a number of molecular features, we observed that several of these MN-expressed genes (the neuronal IgCAM molecule rig-4, the acetylcholine receptor subunits acr-2, acr-5, acr-16, and unc-53, the C. elegans ortholog of the human neuron navigator genes Nav-1/2/3) are expressed in all individual members of a given class.
evidence: Based on expression analysis in this study

claim: The acetylcholine receptor subunits acr-2, acr-5, and acr-16 are expressed in all individual members of a given motor neuron class.
source: Confirming the notion that all neurons of a given class share a number of molecular features, we observed that several of these MN-expressed genes (the neuronal IgCAM molecule rig-4, the acetylcholine receptor subunits acr-2, acr-5, acr-16, and unc-53, the C. elegans ortholog of the human neuron navigator genes Nav-1/2/3) are expressed in all individual members of a given class.
evidence: Based on expression analysis in this study

claim: unc-53 is the C. elegans ortholog of the human neuron navigator genes Nav-1/2/3.
source: Confirming the notion that all neurons of a given class share a number of molecular features, we observed that several of these MN-expressed genes (the neuronal IgCAM molecule rig-4, the acetylcholine receptor subunits acr-2, acr-5, acr-16, and unc-53, the C. elegans ortholog of the human neuron navigator genes Nav-1/2/3) are expressed in all individual members of a given class.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of gene orthology

claim: unc-3 regulates the subclass-specific markers mig-13, itr-1, and glr-4 that are specifically expressed in DA9.
source: We indeed found that unc-3 regulates the subclass-specific mig-13, itr-1 and glr-4 markers that are specifically expressed in the most posterior MN of the DA class located in the preanal ganglion, DA9 (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 2A–B

claim: UNC-3 binding sites (COE motifs) are present in the cis-regulatory regions of DA9-expressed genes.
source: To distinguish between these possibilities, we surveyed the cis-regulatory regions of the DA9-expressed genes and found UNC-3 binding sites (termed 'COE motifs' [Kratsios et al., 2011]), suggesting direct regulation of these MN subclass-specific genes by UNC-3.
evidence: Based on bioinformatic analysis and citation to Kratsios et al., 2011

claim: Small cis-regulatory elements upstream of glr-4 containing the COE motif are sufficient to drive reporter gene expression in DA9.
source: Small pieces of elements upstream of glr-4 and mig-13 that contain the COE motif are sufficient to drive reporter gene expression in DA9 and mutational analysis (glr-4 538 bp COE MUT) shows that the COE motif is essential for this expression (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: Demonstrated through cis-regulatory analysis shown in Figure 2D–E

claim: The COE motif is essential for glr-4 expression in DA9.
source: Small pieces of elements upstream of glr-4 and mig-13 that contain the COE motif are sufficient to drive reporter gene expression in DA9 and mutational analysis (glr-4 538 bp COE MUT) shows that the COE motif is essential for this expression (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: Demonstrated through mutational analysis shown in Figure 2D–E

claim: UNC-3 directly controls the expression of unc-129/TGFβ in DA1-7 neurons.
source: Similarly, UNC-3 directly controls the expression of unc-129/TGFβ, which is expressed in more anteriorly located DA neurons, namely the DA1-7 neurons (Figure 2C and [Kratsios et al., 2011]).
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 2C and supported by citation to Kratsios et al., 2011

claim: unc-3 is required for the expression of the VA12-expressed genes mig-13 and flp-18.
source: Apart from the DA neuron class, unc-3 is also required to regulate subclass-specific genes in the VA neurons, namely the expression of the VA12-expressed genes mig-13 and flp-18, and of del-1, which is expressed in VA1-VA11 neurons (Figure 2B–C and [Kratsios et al., 2011]).
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 2B–C and supported by citation to Kratsios et al., 2011

claim: unc-3 is required for the expression of del-1 in VA1-VA11 neurons.
source: Apart from the DA neuron class, unc-3 is also required to regulate subclass-specific genes in the VA neurons, namely the expression of the VA12-expressed genes mig-13 and flp-18, and of del-1, which is expressed in VA1-VA11 neurons (Figure 2B–C and [Kratsios et al., 2011]).
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 2B–C and supported by citation to Kratsios et al., 2011

claim: Small cis-regulatory elements containing a single COE motif upstream of mig-13 are sufficient to drive reporter gene expression in VA12.
source: Small elements containing a single COE motif upstream of mig-13 are sufficient to drive reporter gene expression in VA12 (Figure 2E).
evidence: Demonstrated through cis-regulatory analysis shown in Figure 2E

claim: unc-3 is required for the expression of avr-15/GluR in AS11.
source: Within the AS neuron class, we find that unc-3 is also required for the expression of avr-15/GluR, a subclass-specific gene expressed in the most posterior AS neuron, AS11 (see further below).
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis in this study

claim: UNC-3 directly controls the expression of motor neuron subclass-specific genes as evidenced by the overrepresentation of COE motifs in their cis-regulatory regions.
source: We conclude that UNC-3 is required for subclass diversity in DA, VA and AS neurons by controlling directly the expression of subclass-specific genes, as evidenced by the overrepresentation of COE motifs in the cis-regulatory region of these genes (Table 1).
evidence: Based on cis-regulatory analysis and data shown in Table 1

claim: unc-3 is expressed in all nine neurons of the DA class and all twelve neurons of the VA class.
source: Since unc-3 is expressed in all nine neurons of the DA class and all twelve neurons of the VA class (Kratsios et al., 2011; Pereira et al., 2015), the question arises why UNC-3 does not activate the subclass-specific genes in all members of a certain class?
evidence: Supported by citations to Kratsios et al., 2011 and Pereira et al., 2015

claim: Three out of six C. elegans Hox genes are differentially expressed in subsets of motor neurons that belong to the same class.
source: We pursued this lead using fosmid-based reporters (fosmids are large genomic clones of ~30 kb that contain all upstream and downstream cis-regulatory elements required for expression of a gene of interest) and found that three out of the six C. elegans Hox genes are differentially expressed in subsets of MNs that belong to the same class (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: Demonstrated through expression analysis using fosmid-based reporters shown in Figure 3A–D

claim: egl-5/Abd-B/Hox9-Hox13 is expressed in the DA9 neuron.
source: Specifically, egl-5/Abd-B/Hox9-Hox13 is expressed in the DA9 neuron, while mab-5/Antp/Hox6-Hox8 is expressed in the DA8 neuron as evidenced by our expression analysis using DA8- and DA9-specifc rfp markers (Figure 3C).
evidence: Demonstrated through expression analysis shown in Figure 3C

claim: mab-5/Antp/Hox6-Hox8 is expressed in the DA8 neuron.
source: Specifically, egl-5/Abd-B/Hox9-Hox13 is expressed in the DA9 neuron, while mab-5/Antp/Hox6-Hox8 is expressed in the DA8 neuron as evidenced by our expression analysis using DA8- and DA9-specifc rfp markers (Figure 3C).
evidence: Demonstrated through expression analysis shown in Figure 3C

claim: lin-39/Dfd/Hox4-Hox5 and mab-5/Antp/Hox6-Hox8 are expressed in more anteriorly located DA neurons.
source: However, lin-39/Dfd/Hox4-Hox5 and mab-5/Antp/Hox6-Hox8 are expressed in more anteriorly located DA neurons (Figure 3B).
evidence: Demonstrated through expression analysis shown in Figure 3B

claim: egl-5 is expressed in VA12 located in the preanal ganglion.
source: Within the VA class, we found that the posterior Hox gene egl-5 is expressed in VA12 (located in the preanal ganglion), while lin-39 and mab-5 are expressed in the more anteriorly located VA neurons along the VNC (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: Demonstrated through expression analysis shown in Figure 3B–C

claim: lin-39 and mab-5 are expressed in more anteriorly located VA neurons along the VNC.
source: Within the VA class, we found that the posterior Hox gene egl-5 is expressed in VA12 (located in the preanal ganglion), while lin-39 and mab-5 are expressed in the more anteriorly located VA neurons along the VNC (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: Demonstrated through expression analysis shown in Figure 3B–C

claim: mab-5 is expressed in AS11, the most posterior AS neuron in the preanal ganglion.
source: Within the AS class, mab-5 is expressed in the most posterior AS neuron, AS11, the only AS neuron in the preanal ganglion, while its expression overlaps with lin-39 in more anterior AS neurons located along the VNC (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: Demonstrated through expression analysis shown in Figure 3B–C

claim: mab-5 expression overlaps with lin-39 in more anterior AS neurons located along the VNC.
source: Within the AS class, mab-5 is expressed in the most posterior AS neuron, AS11, the only AS neuron in the preanal ganglion, while its expression overlaps with lin-39 in more anterior AS neurons located along the VNC (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: Demonstrated through expression analysis shown in Figure 3B–C

claim: Neurons of the DB and VB classes located in the VNC coexpress lin-39 and mab-5.
source: Neurons of the other two classes (DB and VB) located in the VNC (but not the preanal ganglion) also coexpress lin-39 and mab-5 (Figure 3B).
evidence: Demonstrated through expression analysis shown in Figure 3B

claim: Hox single or double null mutant animals show a normal number of cholinergic motor neurons.
source: We find that Hox single or double null mutant animals show a normal number of cholinergic MNs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Hox-deficient motor neurons still express pan-neuronal markers and genes shared by all cholinergic motor neurons.
source: Moreover, Hox-deficient motor neurons still express pan-neuronal markers as well as genes that are shared by all cholinergic MNs (i.e. genes required for acetylcholine synthesis and vesicular packaging)(Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and [Stefanakis et al., 2015]).
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and supported by citation to Stefanakis et al., 2015

claim: The expression of the DA1-7 marker unc-129 is mildly affected in lin-39 null animals.
source: Specifically, the expression of the DA1-7 marker unc-129 is mildly affected in lin-39 null animals, while mab-5 mutants showed no significant effects (Figure 4A).
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 4A

claim: mab-5 mutants show no significant effects on unc-129 expression.
source: Specifically, the expression of the DA1-7 marker unc-129 is mildly affected in lin-39 null animals, while mab-5 mutants showed no significant effects (Figure 4A).
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 4A

claim: lin-39 and mab-5 can function redundantly in C. elegans.
source: Since lin-39 and mab-5 can function redundantly in C. elegans (Liu and Fire, 2000), we generated double mutants and found profound effects on unc-129 expression (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu and Fire, 2000 and demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 4A

claim: lin-39 mab-5 double mutants show profound effects on unc-129 expression.
source: Since lin-39 and mab-5 can function redundantly in C. elegans (Liu and Fire, 2000), we generated double mutants and found profound effects on unc-129 expression (Figure 4A).
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 4A

claim: Animals lacking ceh-20 show similar effects to lin-39 mab-5 double mutants on unc-129 expression.
source: Animals lacking ceh-20, the C. elegans PBX homolog known to function as Hox co-factor (Mann and Chan, 1996; Mann et al., 2009; Merabet and Mann, 2016; Van Auken et al., 2002), show similar effects to lin-39 mab-5 double mutants (Figure 4A).
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 4A and supported by citations to Mann and Chan, 1996; Mann et al., 2009; Merabet and Mann, 2016; Van Auken et al., 2002

claim: ceh-20 is the C. elegans PBX homolog known to function as Hox co-factor.
source: Animals lacking ceh-20, the C. elegans PBX homolog known to function as Hox co-factor (Mann and Chan, 1996; Mann et al., 2009; Merabet and Mann, 2016; Van Auken et al., 2002), show similar effects to lin-39 mab-5 double mutants (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mann and Chan, 1996; Mann et al., 2009; Merabet and Mann, 2016; Van Auken et al., 2002

claim: DA9 specific genes (itr-1, glr-4, mig-13) are controlled by EGL-5.
source: Moreover, DA9 specific-genes (itr-1, glr-4, mig-13) are controlled by EGL-5, although the effects are milder compared to unc-3 null mutants (Figure 4C–E).
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 4C–E

claim: The effects of egl-5 on DA9 specific genes are milder compared to unc-3 null mutants.
source: Moreover, DA9 specific-genes (itr-1, glr-4, mig-13) are controlled by EGL-5, although the effects are milder compared to unc-3 null mutants (Figure 4C–E).
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 4C–E

claim: CEH-20 does not affect the expression of DA9 specific genes.
source: However, CEH-20 does not affect the expression of DA9 specific-genes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), a finding reminiscent of previous reports showing that Abd-B proteins, like EGL-5, can function independently of PBX factors (Rivas et al., 2013; Shen et al., 1997; van Dijk and Murre, 1994).
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and supported by citations to Rivas et al., 2013; Shen et al., 1997; van Dijk and Murre, 1994

claim: Abd-B proteins can function independently of PBX factors.
source: However, CEH-20 does not affect the expression of DA9 specific-genes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), a finding reminiscent of previous reports showing that Abd-B proteins, like EGL-5, can function independently of PBX factors (Rivas et al., 2013; Shen et al., 1997; van Dijk and Murre, 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rivas et al., 2013; Shen et al., 1997; van Dijk and Murre, 1994

claim: egl-5 is expressed in the VA12 neuron and not in other VA neurons along the VNC.
source: egl-5 is expressed in the VA12 neuron (located in the preanal ganglion) and not in other VA neurons along the VNC, and we find that the VA12-expressed genes mig-13 and flp-18 are under the control of egl-5 (Figure 4C–E).
evidence: Demonstrated through expression analysis shown in Figure 4C–E

claim: The VA12-expressed genes mig-13 and flp-18 are under the control of egl-5.
source: egl-5 is expressed in the VA12 neuron (located in the preanal ganglion) and not in other VA neurons along the VNC, and we find that the VA12-expressed genes mig-13 and flp-18 are under the control of egl-5 (Figure 4C–E).
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 4C–E

claim: lin-39 mab-5 double mutants and ceh-20/Pbx null animals affect the expression of del-1 in VA1-VA11 neurons.
source: Similar to the function of lin-39 and mab-5 in the more anteriorly, VNC-located DA neurons, we find that lin-39 mab-5 double mutants, as well as ceh-20/Pbx null animals, affect the expression of del-1, a subclass-specific gene expressed in VA1-VA11 neurons, which is also under the direct control of UNC-3 (Figure 4B).
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 4B

claim: del-1 is under the direct control of UNC-3.
source: Similar to the function of lin-39 and mab-5 in the more anteriorly, VNC-located DA neurons, we find that lin-39 mab-5 double mutants, as well as ceh-20/Pbx null animals, affect the expression of del-1, a subclass-specific gene expressed in VA1-VA11 neurons, which is also under the direct control of UNC-3 (Figure 4B).
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 4B

claim: Expression of lin-39, mab-5, and egl-5 in post-mitotic motor neurons persists into adulthood.
source: Similarly to unc-3, expression of lin-39, mab-5, and egl-5 in post-mitotic MNs persists into adulthood (Figure 3B–C), suggesting that Hox genes may act continuously and cell-autonomously to control MN subclass-specific features in adult stages.
evidence: Demonstrated through expression analysis shown in Figure 3B–C

claim: Hox genes may act continuously and cell-autonomously to control motor neuron subclass-specific features in adult stages.
source: Similarly to unc-3, expression of lin-39, mab-5, and egl-5 in post-mitotic MNs persists into adulthood (Figure 3B–C), suggesting that Hox genes may act continuously and cell-autonomously to control MN subclass-specific features in adult stages.
evidence: Inferred from persistent expression of Hox genes into adulthood

claim: LIN-39 binds onto its own cis-regulatory region.
source: Biochemical studies have indeed identified that LIN-39 binds onto its own cis-regulatory region (Niu et al., 2011), suggesting that it maintains its own expression through positive autoregulation.
evidence: Supported by citation to Niu et al., 2011

claim: LIN-39 maintains its own expression through positive autoregulation.
source: Biochemical studies have indeed identified that LIN-39 binds onto its own cis-regulatory region (Niu et al., 2011), suggesting that it maintains its own expression through positive autoregulation.
evidence: Inferred from LIN-39 binding to its own cis-regulatory region

claim: The expression of egl-5, lin-39, and mab-5 is not affected in unc-3 null mutants.
source: To distinguish between these two possibilities, we first monitored the expression of egl-5, lin-39, and mab-5 fosmid-based reporters in unc-3 null mutants. We did not detect any defects (Figure 5A).
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 5A

claim: The expression of unc-3 is not affected in egl-5 mutants.
source: Conversely, the expression of unc-3 is not affected in egl-5 mutants (Figure 5B), suggesting that unc-3 and Hox proteins may act in parallel pathways that function synergistically to control MN subclass-specific gene expression.
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 5B

claim: unc-3 and Hox proteins may act in parallel pathways that function synergistically to control motor neuron subclass-specific gene expression.
source: Conversely, the expression of unc-3 is not affected in egl-5 mutants (Figure 5B), suggesting that unc-3 and Hox proteins may act in parallel pathways that function synergistically to control MN subclass-specific gene expression.
evidence: Inferred from lack of cross-regulatory interactions

claim: Hox genes do not affect the expression of ACh pathway genes (VAChT, ChAT, ChT).
source: The notion of independence is further supported by the lack of an effect of Hox genes on the expression of ACh pathway genes (VAChT, ChAT, ChT), which are direct UNC-3 target genes in all MNs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: ACh pathway genes (VAChT, ChAT, ChT) are direct UNC-3 target genes in all motor neurons.
source: The notion of independence is further supported by the lack of an effect of Hox genes on the expression of ACh pathway genes (VAChT, ChAT, ChT), which are direct UNC-3 target genes in all MNs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on established knowledge from previous studies

claim: unc-3(fp8); lin-39 mab-5 triple mutants display a more severe effect on unc-129 and del-1 expression compared to lin-39 mab-5 double or unc-3(fp8) single mutants.
source: We find that unc-3(fp8); lin-39 mab-5 triple mutants display a more severe effect on unc-129 and del-1 expression when compared to lin-39 mab-5 double or unc-3(fp8) single mutants (Figure 5C–D).
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 5C–D

claim: UNC-3 and Hox factors act synergistically to generate DA and VA subclass diversity.
source: To sum up, the stronger effects on unc-129 and del-1 expression in unc-3(fp8); lin-39 mab-5 triple mutants together with the absence of cross-regulatory interactions between UNC-3 and Hox lead us to conclude that these regulatory factors act synergistically to generate DA and VA subclass diversity by controlling the expression of subclass-specific genes.
evidence: Inferred from genetic analysis showing additive effects in triple mutants

claim: The GATTGATG sequence is a putative binding site for LIN-39 in C. elegans cells.
source: Despite lacking cell-type specificity, these ChIP-seq studies have identified the GATTGATG sequence as a putative binding site for LIN-39 in C. elegans cells (Figure 6A).
evidence: Based on ChIP-seq data from modENCODE project

claim: Copies of the LIN-39 motif and COE motif are present in minimal cis-regulatory elements of unc-129 and del-1.
source: Focusing on two of the subclass-specific markers, unc-129 and del-1, we found copies of this LIN-39 motif (as well as copies of the UNC-3 binding site, termed COE motif) in minimal cis-regulatory elements (243 bp for unc-129 and 488 bp for del-1) that drive reporter gene expression in DA1-7/DB and VA1-11/VB MNs, respectively (Figure 6B,E).
evidence: Based on bioinformatic analysis and cis-regulatory analysis shown in Figure 6B,E

claim: Mutation of LIN-39 sites in the unc-129 element results in dramatic loss of reporter gene expression in DA1-7 and DB neurons.
source: To test the functionality of the putative LIN-39 sites (GATTGATG), we mutated these sites in the unc-129 element (243 bp LIN-39 SITES 6 & 7 MUT) and observed a dramatic loss of reporter gene expression in the DA1-7 and DB neurons (Figure 6B–D), which phenocopies the effect observed in lin-39 mab-5 double mutants (Figure 4A).
evidence: Demonstrated through mutational analysis shown in Figure 6B–D

claim: ChIP-seq data show adjacent binding for LIN-39 and MAB-5 on the unc-129 243 bp region.
source: ChIP-seq data from the modENCODE consortium show adjacent binding for LIN-39 (as well as MAB-5) on the unc-129_243 bp region that we have defined through our cis-regulatory analysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1)(Boyle et al., 2014; Niu et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Boyle et al., 2014 and Niu et al., 2011, and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: Mutation of one LIN-39 site in the del-1 element results in reduction of reporter gene expression in VA1-11 and VB neurons.
source: Moreover, mutation of one LIN-39 site in the del-1 element (488 bp LIN-39 SITE 4 MUT) resulted in a reduction of reporter gene expression in VA1-11 and VB neurons (Figure 6E–F).
evidence: Demonstrated through mutational analysis shown in Figure 6E–F

claim: LIN-39 directly controls expression of the motor neuron subclass-specific genes unc-129 and del-1 through a discrete cis-regulatory motif.
source: Altogether, our findings suggest that, similar to UNC-3, the Hox protein LIN-39 (possibly together with MAB-5) directly controls expression of the MN subclass-specific genes unc-129 and del-1 through a discrete cis-regulatory motif (Figure 5E).
evidence: Inferred from cis-regulatory analysis and mutational studies

claim: In egl-5 mutants, 100% display del-1 de-repression in VA12.
source: We found that 100% of egl-5 mutants display del-1 de-repression in VA12, while in 84.2% of egl-5 mutants unc-129 is de-repressed in DA9 (Figure 7A).
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 7A

claim: In 84.2% of egl-5 mutants, unc-129 is de-repressed in DA9.
source: We found that 100% of egl-5 mutants display del-1 de-repression in VA12, while in 84.2% of egl-5 mutants unc-129 is de-repressed in DA9 (Figure 7A).
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 7A

claim: egl-5 promotes posterior motor neuron subclass identity and represses more anterior motor neuron subclass identity.
source: Hence, egl-5 promotes posterior MN subclass identity and represses more anterior MN subclass identity.
evidence: Inferred from de-repression of anterior markers in posterior neurons in egl-5 mutants

claim: Mis-expression of egl-5 in all DA neurons results in partial rescue of unc-129 de-repression in DA9 of egl-5 mutants.
source: Mis-expression of egl-5 in all 9 DA neurons (DA1-9) (using a fragment of the unc-4 promoter, Ex [unc-4prom::egl-5]) results in partial rescue of unc-129 de-repression in DA9 of egl-5 mutants.
evidence: Demonstrated through rescue experiment shown in Figure 7B

claim: Mis-expression of egl-5 in all DA neurons results in repression of unc-129 expression in anterior DA neurons (DA1-7).
source: In addition, mis-expression of egl-5 in all 9 DA neurons results in repression of unc-129 expression in anterior DA neurons (DA1-7), demonstrating that EGL-5 is also sufficient to repress unc-129 expression.
evidence: Demonstrated through mis-expression experiment shown in Figure 7B

claim: EGL-5 is sufficient to repress unc-129 expression.
source: Since EGL-5 is required for repressing unc-129 in DA9, we also performed a sufficiency experiment where we misexpressed EGL-5 in DA1-7 neurons along the VNC and indeed found that EGL-5 is sufficient to repress unc-129 expression in these neurons (Figure 7B).
evidence: Demonstrated through mis-expression experiment shown in Figure 7B

claim: EGL-5 acts cell autonomously.
source: As the promoter (unc-4) we used to drive egl-5 expression is also expressed in DA9, we observed partial rescue of unc-129 de-repression in DA9 of egl-5 null animals, indicating that EGL-5 acts cell autonomously (Figure 7B).
evidence: Demonstrated through rescue experiment shown in Figure 7B

claim: EGL-5 has a dual role in DA9 and VA12 neurons: activating subclass-specific genes and repressing anterior subclass features.
source: We conclude that EGL-5 has a dual role in DA9 and VA12 neurons. Apart from working together with UNC-3 to activate the expression of DA9- and VA12-specific genes (Figure 4C–E, model in Figure 5E), EGL-5 is also required to repress features associated with DA1-7 and VA1-11 neurons located more anteriorly (Figure 7A).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing both activation and repression functions

claim: lin-39 is de-repressed in DA9 and VA12 neurons in 100% of egl-5 mutant animals.
source: We find no evidence for mab-5 de-repression (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), but we observed lin-39 de-repression in the DA9 and VA12 neurons in 100% of egl-5 mutant animals (Figure 7C).
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 7C

claim: The posterior Hox gene egl-5 represses the mid-body Hox gene lin-39 in DA9 and VA12 neurons.
source: Consistent with these reports, our analysis demonstrates, with single-neuron resolution, that the posterior Hox gene egl-5 represses the mid-body Hox gene lin-39 in DA9 and VA12 neurons.
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis showing lin-39 de-repression in egl-5 mutants

claim: egl-5 expression is not affected in motor neurons of lin-39 mab-5 animals.
source: However, we found no differences when we monitored egl-5 expression in MNs of lin-39 mab-5 animals (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1

claim: Loss of egl-5 results in misplacement of DA9 neuromuscular synapses such that they are located more anteriorly in the dorsal nerve cord.
source: We find that loss of egl-5 results in misplacement of the DA9 neuromuscular synapses such that they are located more anteriorly in the DNC, in a territory normally reserved for neuromuscular synapses of more anteriorly located DA neurons (Figure 8A).
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 8A

claim: EGL-5 functions cell-autonomously to control aspects of DA9 identity.
source: These defects can be partially rescued by driving egl-5 expression specifically in DA9 using the glr-4 promoter which is partially affected by egl-5 (Figure 4D), indicating that EGL-5 functions cell-autonomously to control aspects of DA9 identity (Figure 8A).
evidence: Demonstrated through rescue experiment shown in Figure 8A

claim: In adult egl-5 mutants, the synaptic input from AVG to DA9 is lost.
source: We find that in adult egl-5 mutants, this synaptic input is lost, consistent with the neuron adopting the identity of a more anterior DA neuron (Figure 8B).
evidence: Demonstrated through GRASP analysis shown in Figure 8B

claim: The initial establishment of the AVG to DA9 synaptic input is unaffected in egl-5 mutants.
source: The initial establishment of the synaptic input is, however, unaffected (L1 stage in Figure 8B), suggesting that egl-5 controls maintenance of subclass-specific synaptic connectivity.
evidence: Demonstrated through GRASP analysis at L1 stage shown in Figure 8B

claim: egl-5 controls maintenance of subclass-specific synaptic connectivity.
source: The initial establishment of the synaptic input is, however, unaffected (L1 stage in Figure 8B), suggesting that egl-5 controls maintenance of subclass-specific synaptic connectivity.
evidence: Inferred from loss of synaptic input in adults but not at L1 stage in egl-5 mutants

claim: A Hox gene controls motor neuron subclass-specific synaptic wiring patterns.
source: Taken together, our analysis therefore demonstrates that a Hox gene not only controls molecular markers, but may also control MN subclass-specific synaptic wiring patterns.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing egl-5 effects on synaptic connectivity

claim: The expression of the DA1-7 marker unc-129 is de-repressed in DA8 neurons of mab-5 mutants.
source: We indeed found that – similarly to the effect of EGL-5 in DA9 neurons – the expression of the DA1-7 marker unc-129 is de-repressed in DA8 neurons of mab-5 mutants (Figure 9A–B).
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 9A–B

claim: The DA9-specific markers mig-13, glr-4 and itr-1 are de-repressed in the DA8 neuron of mab-5 mutants.
source: DA8 not only adopts features of the more anterior DA neurons, but, unexpectedly, it also adopts features of the more posterior DA9 neuron. Specifically, the DA9-specific markers mig-13, glr-4 and itr-1 are de-repressed in the DA8 neuron of mab-5(-) animals (Figure 9A–B)(Sym et al., 1999).
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 9A–B and supported by citation to Sym et al., 1999

claim: mab-5 binds to the cis-regulatory region of mig-13 and itr-1.
source: ChIP-sequencing results from the modENCODE project demonstrate that mab-5 binds to the cis-regulatory region of mig-13 and itr-1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), indicating that mab-5 may directly repress the expression of these DA9-specific genes in the DA8 neuron.
evidence: Based on ChIP-seq data from modENCODE project shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: mab-5 may directly repress the expression of DA9-specific genes in the DA8 neuron.
source: ChIP-sequencing results from the modENCODE project demonstrate that mab-5 binds to the cis-regulatory region of mig-13 and itr-1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), indicating that mab-5 may directly repress the expression of these DA9-specific genes in the DA8 neuron.
evidence: Inferred from mab-5 binding to cis-regulatory regions and de-repression in mab-5 mutants

claim: mab-5 ensures the adoption of DA8 fate by preventing the expression of DA1-7-specific and DA9-specific features.
source: Taken together, our results show that mab-5 ensures the adoption of DA8 fate by preventing the expression of DA1-7-specific and DA9-specific features (Figure 9C).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing de-repression of both anterior and posterior markers in mab-5 mutants

claim: In the absence of mab-5, the DA8 neuron adopts a 'mixed' fate characterized by DA1-7 and DA9 traits.
source: Hence, in the absence of mab-5, the DA8 neuron adopts a 'mixed' fate characterized by DA1-7 and DA9 traits.
evidence: Inferred from de-repression of both DA1-7 and DA9 markers in DA8 of mab-5 mutants

claim: The terminal selector unc-3 and the Hox gene mab-5 control avr-15/GluR expression in VA11 and AS11 neurons.
source: We find that mab-5 is required for avr-15/GluR expression in VA11 and AS11 neurons (Figure 9D–E). unc-3 is also required for avr-15/GluR (Figure 9D–E), thereby again corroborating the theme of unc-3 cooperating with Hox genes in motor neuron subclass specification.
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 9D–E

claim: UNC-3 and HOX genes collaborate to control the expression of intermediary regulatory factors.
source: The data described above indicates a direct collaboration of the UNC-3 terminal selector with Hox genes in specific motor neuron subclasses on the cis-regulatory level of 'nuts and bolts' effector genes that define specific cellular phenotypes. We also found evidence for a collaboration of UNC-3 with HOX genes in controlling the expression of intermediary regulatory factors.
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis in this study

claim: cfi-1 is expressed in DA1-DA8 motor neurons but not in DA9.
source: For example, the ARID-type transcription factor cfi-1 is expressed in the DA1-DA8 MNs, but not in DA9 (Figure 1B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1B

claim: cfi-1 expression is controlled by unc-3.
source: cfi-1 expression is controlled by unc-3 (Kerk et al., 2017) and we investigated the impact of HOX genes on the subclass specificity of cfi-1 expression.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kerk et al., 2017

claim: lin-39 and mab-5 are jointly required to activate cfi-1 in DA1-DA8.
source: We found that the DA9-expressed gene egl-5 is not involved in restricting cfi-1 to DA1-8, but rather lin-39 and mab-5 are jointly required to activate cfi-1 in DA1-DA8 (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1

claim: The ionotropic glutamate receptor glr-4 becomes derepressed in DA1-DA8 in cfi-1 mutants.
source: The ionotropic glutamate receptor glr-4, normally expressed only in the SAB neurons and the DA9 subclass neuron, becomes derepressed in the remaining DA neurons (DA1-DA8) in cfi-1 mutants (Kerk et al., 2017) and, consequently, also in lin-39 mab-5 mutants (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1 and supported by citation to Kerk et al., 2017

claim: cfi-1 regulation by lin-39 and mab-5 is HOX gene- and cell-specific.
source: cfi-1 regulation by lin-39 and mab-5 is HOX gene- and cell-specific, since the posterior HOX gene egl-5 does not affect cfi-1 expression, i.e. we observed no de-repression of cfi-1 in the DA9 neuron of egl-5 mutants (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1

claim: There is no cross-regulatory relationship between cfi-1 and HOX genes.
source: There is no cross-regulatory relationship between cfi-1 and HOX genes, since HOX gene expression is unaffected in cfi-1 mutants (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1

claim: bnc-1 is expressed in all VA and VB neurons except the anterior-most VB neuron VB1.
source: A similar effect of HOX genes can also be observed on the expression of another MN class-specific repressor, bnc-1. This Zn finger transcription factor is expressed in VA/VB MNs, is a direct target of UNC-3, and antagonizes the activity of UNC-3 on a number of effector genes in VA/VB (Kerk et al., 2017). bnc-1 is expressed in all VA and VB neurons, except the anterior-most VB neuron VB1.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kerk et al., 2017 and demonstrated through expression analysis

claim: bnc-1 is a direct target of UNC-3.
source: This Zn finger transcription factor is expressed in VA/VB MNs, is a direct target of UNC-3, and antagonizes the activity of UNC-3 on a number of effector genes in VA/VB (Kerk et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kerk et al., 2017

claim: bnc-1 antagonizes the activity of UNC-3 on a number of effector genes in VA/VB.
source: This Zn finger transcription factor is expressed in VA/VB MNs, is a direct target of UNC-3, and antagonizes the activity of UNC-3 on a number of effector genes in VA/VB (Kerk et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kerk et al., 2017

claim: In lin-39 mab-5 mutants, bnc-1 expression is diminished in motor neurons in the midbody region.
source: We indeed found that in lin-39 mab-5 mutants, bnc-1 expression is diminished in MNs in the midbody region (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1

claim: unc-3 and HOX genes collaborate to regulate the expression of intermediary regulatory factors.
source: In conclusion, unc-3 and HOX genes collaborate not only on the regulation of terminal effector genes that define terminal cellular phenotypes, but they also collaborate to regulate the expression of intermediary regulatory factors.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing HOX gene effects on cfi-1 and bnc-1 expression

claim: An intersectional gene regulatory strategy of distinct Hox genes and a broadly-acting transcription factor generates neuronal subclass diversity.
source: We provide here insights into the problem of how anatomically and functionally defined neuron classes diversify into specialized subclasses. Although the molecular mechanisms that generate interclass diversity, that is, differences between neuron classes, are beginning to be uncovered in multiple distinct systems, the mechanisms of subclass diversification have remained more elusive.
evidence: Main conclusion of the study based on experimental data

claim: The terminal selector UNC-3 controls features shared by all motor neuron class members and is also required for subclass diversification.
source: First, we find that the terminal selector-type transcription factor UNC-3 – apart from controlling features shared by all MN class members – is also required for subclass diversification by regulating the expression of MN subclass-specific genes.
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis in this study

claim: Three C. elegans Hox genes act synergistically and cooperate with UNC-3 in an intersectional manner to control the expression of motor neuron subclass-specific genes along the anterior-posterior axis.
source: Third, we uncovered that the posterior Hox gene egl-5/Abd-B/ Hox9-Hox13, apart from acting as an UNC-3 co-activator to generate MN subclass diversity, is also required to repress the expression of the mid-body Hox gene lin-39/Scr/Dfd/Hox4-Hox5, while the Hox gene, mab-5/Antp/Hox6-Hox8, may operate as both an activator and repressor directly on its effector genes.
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis in this study

claim: The posterior Hox gene egl-5 is required to repress the expression of the mid-body Hox gene lin-39.
source: Third, we uncovered that the posterior Hox gene egl-5/Abd-B/ Hox9-Hox13, apart from acting as an UNC-3 co-activator to generate MN subclass diversity, is also required to repress the expression of the mid-body Hox gene lin-39/Scr/Dfd/Hox4-Hox5, while the Hox gene, mab-5/Antp/Hox6-Hox8, may operate as both an activator and repressor directly on its effector genes.
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis in this study

claim: The Hox gene mab-5 may operate as both an activator and repressor directly on its effector genes.
source: Third, we uncovered that the posterior Hox gene egl-5/Abd-B/ Hox9-Hox13, apart from acting as an UNC-3 co-activator to generate MN subclass diversity, is also required to repress the expression of the mid-body Hox gene lin-39/Scr/Dfd/Hox4-Hox5, while the Hox gene, mab-5/Antp/Hox6-Hox8, may operate as both an activator and repressor directly on its effector genes.
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis in this study

claim: The intersectional activity of a single, broadly-acting terminal selector and distinct Hox genes constitutes a conceptually straightforward solution to how neuronal subclass diversity is generated along the anterior-posterior axis.
source: Hence, the intersectional activity of a single, broadly-acting terminal selector and distinct Hox genes may constitute a conceptually straightforward solution to the intriguing problem of how neuronal subclass diversity is generated along the A-P axis of the nervous system.
evidence: Main conclusion of the study based on experimental data

claim: Diversification of distinct C. elegans motor neuron classes involves class-specific direct repression of effector genes.
source: Recent work has demonstrated that diversification of distinct C. elegans MN classes (i.e. interclass diversification) involves class-specific direct repression of effector genes (Kerk et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kerk et al., 2017

claim: Motor neuron subclass diversity is mainly generated through positive regulatory inputs provided by UNC-3 and Hox proteins to subclass-specific effector genes.
source: In contrast, our genetic and cis-regulatory analyses show that MN subclass diversity ("intraclass diversity") is mainly generated through positive regulatory inputs provided by UNC-3 and Hox proteins to subclass-specific effector genes (Figure 10).
evidence: Demonstrated through genetic and cis-regulatory analyses in this study

claim: Hox proteins can be considered as 'sub-selectors' because they selectively regulate motor neuron subclass-specific features.
source: By analogy to the terminal selector function of UNC-3 that controls shared (Kratsios et al., 2015, 2011), class-specific (Kratsios et al., 2015, 2011) and subclass-specific (this study) features of MNs throughout life, Hox proteins can be considered as 'sub-selectors' because they selectively regulate MN subclass-specific features.
evidence: Conceptual inference based on experimental data

claim: The diversification of the SAB class of head motor neurons and ASE class of gustatory neurons in C. elegans relies on direct repression of subclass-specific effector genes.
source: This regulatory principle of co-activation of subclass-specific genes is certainly not the only mechanism to achieve neuronal subclass diversity. For example, the diversification of the SAB class of head MNs and ASE class of gustatory neurons in C. elegans relies on direct repression of subclass-specific effector genes (Etchberger et al., 2009; Kerk et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Etchberger et al., 2009 and Kerk et al., 2017

claim: Hox genes are required for neuronal diversity, cell survival, axonal pathfinding and circuit assembly.
source: Collectively, this large body of work has established that Hox genes are required for neuronal diversity, cell survival, axonal pathfinding and circuit assembly.
evidence: Based on established knowledge from multiple studies

claim: Only a handful of Hox downstream targets have been identified in the nervous system to date.
source: However, only a handful of Hox downstream targets have been identified in the nervous system to date and the mechanistic details of how Hox genes interact with other transcription factors during neuronal development remained ill-defined.
evidence: Based on review of existing literature

claim: Seven effector genes and two intermediary regulatory factors (cfi-1 and bnc-1) are Hox downstream targets.
source: Our findings provide novel insights on the molecular mechanisms employed by Hox genes to control neuronal diversity: (i) by identifying seven effector genes and two intermediary regulatory factors (cfi-1 and bnc-1) as Hox downstream targets and (ii) by demonstrating that distinct Hox genes intersect with a broadly-acting, terminal selector-type transcription factor and act together at the cis-regulatory level of effector genes to generate MN subclass diversity.
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis in this study

claim: Hox genes control the expression of motor neuron subclass-specific genes during development and may maintain effector gene expression or serve additional roles in adult life.
source: Given the maintained expression of Hox genes in adult C. elegans MNs and mouse CNS (Hutlet et al., 2016), we surmise that Hox genes, apart from controlling the expression of MN subclass-specific genes during development, may also maintain effector gene expression or serve additional roles in adult life.
evidence: Inferred from maintained expression of Hox genes in adults and supported by citation to Hutlet et al., 2016

claim: egl-5 is required for the maintenance (not the initial formation) of the synaptic input that the DA9 motor neuron receives from AVG interneurons.
source: We indeed uncovered an unexpected role for the posterior Hox gene egl-5/Abd-B/Hox9-Hox13 in adult animals, as egl-5/Abd-B/Hox9-Hox13 is required for the maintenance (not the initial formation) of the synaptic input that the DA9 MN receives from AVG interneurons.
evidence: Demonstrated through GRASP analysis in this study

claim: Hox genes are required for synaptic input received by motor neurons.
source: Apart from adding a temporal dimension to the function of egl-5/Abd-B/Hox9-Hox13, these findings also demonstrate that Hox genes are required for synaptic input received by MNs, extending previous reports on the requirement of Hox genes for MN to muscle connectivity (Catela et al., 2015, 2016; Friedrich et al., 2016; Hessinger et al., 2017; Philippidou and Dasen, 2013).
evidence: Demonstrated through experimental analysis in this study and supported by citations to Catela et al., 2015, 2016; Friedrich et al., 2016; Hessinger et al., 2017; Philippidou and Dasen, 2013

claim: EGL-5 represses the expression of lin-39 in posterior touch sensory neurons in C. elegans.
source: Supporting the generality of this dual mechanism of action, a recent study demonstrated a similar, dual role for EGL-5 in the diversification of posterior touch sensory neurons in C.elegans (Zheng et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zheng et al., 2015

claim: The posterior Hox genes Hoxa10, Hoxc10, and Hoxd10 in the mouse spinal cord are required for the acquisition of posterior motor neuron fate and for repression of anterior motor neuron identity.
source: Moreover, the posterior Hox genes Hoxa10, Hoxc10, and Hoxd10 in the mouse spinal cord appear to function in a similar manner since they are required not only for the acquisition of posterior MN fate but also for repression of anterior MN identity (Hostikka et al., 2009; Lin and Carpenter, 2003; Wahba et al., 2001; Wu et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hostikka et al., 2009; Lin and Carpenter, 2003; Wahba et al., 2001; Wu et al., 2008

claim: Posterior Hox genes diversify posterior neurons from their more anterior counterparts.
source: This dual mechanism of posterior Hox gene action may explain how neuronal subclass diversity arises from an evolutionary standpoint, i.e. posterior Hox genes diversify posterior neurons from their more anterior counterparts.
evidence: Speculative inference based on experimental data

claim: Homeotic transformations associated with Hox gene mutations have been proposed as a potential source of novelty at the single cell level that could contribute to the evolution of neuronal diversity.
source: Supporting this possibility, homeotic transformations associated with Hox gene mutations have been proposed as a potential source of novelty at the single cell level that could contribute to the evolution of neuronal diversity (Arlotta and Hobert, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Arlotta and Hobert, 2015

claim: Epidermal growth factor (EGF) signaling from a neighboring cell to the P12 neuroblast is necessary for the initiation of egl-5 expression in P12.
source: The signals that initiate lin-39 and mab-5 expression in VNC MNs are not clear, but it has been shown that epidermal growth factor (EGF) signaling from a neighboring cell to the P12 neuroblast (which produces the VA12 neuron) is necessary for the initiation of egl-5 expression in P12 (Jiang and Sternberg, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jiang and Sternberg, 1998

claim: Ebf2 is co-expressed with distinct Hox genes in medial motor column (MMC) motor neurons along the anterior-posterior axis of the mouse spinal cord.
source: We found that Ebf2, one of the four unc-3 mouse orthologs, is co-expressed with distinct Hox genes in medial motor column (MMC) MNs along the A-P axis of the mouse spinal cord (Figure 10—figure supplements 1 and 2), leading us to speculate that Ebf2 and Hox may work together to generate MMC subclass diversity along the A-P axis, which is perhaps essential for innervation of distinct body wall (axial) muscles.
evidence: Demonstrated through expression analysis shown in Figure 10—figure supplements 1 and 2

claim: Ebf2 and Hox may work together to generate MMC subclass diversity along the anterior-posterior axis.
source: We found that Ebf2, one of the four unc-3 mouse orthologs, is co-expressed with distinct Hox genes in medial motor column (MMC) MNs along the A-P axis of the mouse spinal cord (Figure 10—figure supplements 1 and 2), leading us to speculate that Ebf2 and Hox may work together to generate MMC subclass diversity along the A-P axis, which is perhaps essential for innervation of distinct body wall (axial) muscles.
evidence: Speculative inference based on co-expression data

claim: Hox genes and the transcription factor FoxP1 are essential for diversification of spinal motor neurons of the lateral motor column (LMC) population.
source: Intriguingly, Hox genes and the transcription factor, FoxP1, are essential for diversification of spinal MNs of the lateral motor column (LMC) population, although the direct downstream effector genes of FoxP1 and Hox are largely unknown (Dasen et al., 2008; Rousso et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dasen et al., 2008 and Rousso et al., 2008

claim: The expression of distinct Hox genes intersects with the broadly-acting transcription factor Pet-1 in molecularly and functionally distinct populations of serotonergic neurons in the mouse brainstem.
source: Moving beyond MNs, a recent study on the molecular deconstruction of the serotonergic system in the mouse brainstem has revealed that the expression of distinct Hox genes intersects with the broadly-acting transcription factor Pet-1 in molecularly and functionally distinct populations of serotonergic neurons (Okaty et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Okaty et al., 2015

claim: The intersectional gene regulatory principle may be utilized for the fractionation of neuronal classes into subclasses.
source: We propose that this intersectional gene regulatory principle may be utilized for the fractionation of neuronal classes into subclasses.
evidence: Proposed based on findings in this study and other systems

claim: Fractionation of neuronal classes into subclasses is essential for the acquisition of subclass-specific traits, which could ultimately lead to the evolution of novel neuron types and circuits.
source: Such fractionation is essential for the acquisition of subclass-specific traits, which could ultimately lead to the evolution of novel neuron types and circuits.
evidence: Speculative inference about evolutionary implications
